newsitem.title: USA: Rubin says no reason to expect big Treasury sales.
newsitem.headline: Rubin says no reason to expect big Treasury sales.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Wednesday that he saw no reason to expect concerted sales of U.S. Treasury securities and voiced confidence U.S. markets could absorb them if they occurred.

"Our markets are so deep and so broad that even if there was enormous concerted selling by a foreign country -- I have no reason to think it would occur -- our markets could absorb it readily," Rubin told reporters.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto rocked U.S. financial markets on Monday when he seemed to suggest that Japan might sell U.S. Treasuries and buy gold if Washington did not cooperate with Tokyo to stabilize currencies.
Rubin acknowledged that there might be a brief period of disruption in markets, if there was concerted selling, before calm returned.
"The key is to make sure that we have the kind of policies in this country that will cause investors around the world to believe in this country," Rubin said.
He called U.S. economic conditions "very good" and said that they were likely to remain good, adding that markets over time reflect fundamentals.

"As long as we are fiscally responsible, as long as we have a sound currency, as long as we pursue sensible and sound economic policies, this is a place where people are going to want to invest," Rubin said.

Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said that recent heavy capital inflows into the United States had been used to finance investment and thus did not raise the kind of concerns they might have in the past.

"The capital flows....are driven by the need to finance investment," Sunmmers said. "That equipment (investment) is raising the productivity of American workers and is an important part of strong export performance."

Asked if the Japanese government had provided the Clinton administration with any clarification of Hashimoto's remarks, Summers referred to a statement issued by Japanese finance ministry official Takatoshi Kato.

Kato, who is Vice Finance Minister for International Affairs, said that Japan would continue to cooperate with the United States to stabilize foreign exchange rates. He also said Hashimoto regretted that his remarks had been misread.
"Mr Kato's statement clarifying the Prime Minister's remarks speaks for itself," Summers said.
